text: The old books hand down a severe picture for the first face of Leo: a man astride a lion, and a list of meanings that flatters no one, boldness tipped into violence, appetite, cruelty, and labors that must be borne. Saturn is the ruler the tradition assigns these ten degrees, and the whole face lives in the tension between mount and rider. Something in you wants with unusual force here. The Lion's heat does not come in flickers; it arrives as a hunger that stays, for recognition, for pleasure, for the feel of being stronger than the task in front of you. Left to itself, that hunger can run rough over your own body, your own people, your own better judgment, and the old writers were blunt about that failure. Their bluntness is worth keeping. But the picture holds two figures, not one. The rider is the part of you that can grip the mane and pick a direction. When appetite and discipline take turns, this face gives a staying power that gentler degrees never learn: you can carry a heavy want for years without dropping it or being dragged by it. The labor the books mention becomes the kind you chose, and that choice is the whole difference.

Dignity under challenge is the climate of the middle face of Leo. Jupiter is the Chaldean ruler of these ten degrees. The old image matches him oddly: a crowned figure with hands raised, a drawn sword in one fist and a shield in the other, his face set in a threat. The books read him as hidden contention and unknown victory, quarrels, and the occasions of battle. You know the posture. Your pride is not the sunny kind that assumes applause; it expects a rival. You notice who is positioning against you before anyone says a word, and you are often right. At work this makes you formidable in any contest that matters. In love it can make you tiring, because a raised voice from someone you trust reaches your sword arm before it reaches your ears. Yet the crown in the picture is real: you win more of these fights than you ever mention, and the quiet victories build you most. Study the shield. A ruler who only knows the sword ends up fighting servants, and your gift here is rarer: defending what matters without needing the war.

Mars ruling the last face of Leo sounds like a war drum until you read what the tradition actually says about it. The old picture shows two figures, a young man carrying a whip and beside him a man worn down to sadness, and the meaning the books attach is startling for Mars: love, society, and the loss of your own right for the sake of avoiding a fight. That is the exact tension you live with here. Your warmth is not soft; it is driven. You pursue the people you love, you organize the gathering, you throw yourself into loyalty the way the Lion throws itself into everything, fully. And you know the second figure too. Keeping the pride together can cost you your claim: the apology you offered just to end it, the share you stopped asking for, the want you swallowed because harmony felt more important. Sometimes it is more important. Your generosity, like the young man's whip, has force behind it, and force is allowed to set terms. Maturity here looks like warmth that stops paying for peace with pieces of yourself, and the people around you learn that your company and your standards arrive together.

Plenty has a technique, and the first face of Virgo is where the Virgin learns it. The Sun rules these degrees, and the old books give them a pair of plain figures: a good maid, and a man scattering seed on ploughed ground. Their meaning is just as plain, and just as large. This is the part of the sign where your work turns fruitful: getting wealth, ordering a household and a table, sowing what later feeds everyone. You have a feel for the unglamorous sequence that makes plenty happen, the preparation, the timing, the small daily disciplines other people skip. Competence is not a performance for you; it is closer to a bodily habit, and you are happiest with your hands in the task. The Sun adds a twist. Some part of you wants the work to be seen, and you may feel a quiet sting when the harvest is praised and the sower is not. Watch that accounting. The maid and the sower in the old picture are not posing; they are doing the thing everything else depends on. Your standing grows when you claim the results of your skill out loud, without waiting for someone else to notice that the field is full because you planted it.

Two figures stand in the old picture of Virgo's middle face: a man dressed in a rough skin, and a shaggy-haired man gripping a bag. Venus is the ruler here, and the books do not mince words about the meaning: gain, the scraping together of wealth, and covetousness. Before you wince at the last word, sit with the first two. Here, love takes the form of having enough. You care about things well made and well kept. You know what you have, down to the last shelf, and there is real pleasure for you in a stocked pantry, a mended coat, an account that balances. Venus makes it sensual: texture, fit, the right weight of a tool in your hand. The bag tells the harder story: the same instinct that gathers beautifully can close its fist, counting instead of enjoying, keeping past need, letting the fear of not-enough tax every pleasure. You may also catch yourself handing over things when what was asked for was you. You steady as the bag opens. Wealth you can feel, share, and use is the kind this part of the sign was always after.

Mercury, which rules Virgo itself, also rules the sign's last face, and here the tradition turns somber. Its picture for these degrees is a deaf woman dressed in white, or an old man leaning on a staff, and the books attach weakness, depletion, and things falling quietly out of use. Take that weight as the old writers' honesty about endings, not as a verdict on you. What these degrees describe is the Virgin's mind meeting its limits. You see what is wearing out before anyone else does: the plan with the flaw in it, the work that has gone as far as it can, the tree that will not bear again. That sight is a real faculty, and it can make you the person trusted with endings, the careful closing of what is finished. Its cost is a certain loneliness, a habit of expecting decline, a weariness that comes from noticing everything. The staff in the old man's hand cuts both ways. It says some things cannot be carried, and it says support exists for the carrying that remains. You do well here when your clear sight serves timing rather than dread, when you know when to mend and when to lay a thing down with respect.

The first face of Libra is justice with its sleeves rolled up. The Moon is the face's ruler, and the old picture pairs an angry man holding a pipe with a man quietly reading a book, which the books explain as the power to justify and help the weak against the powerful and wicked. Two things live together in you here: feeling and argument. Unfairness hits you in the body before you have words for it, and then the words come, careful ones, because some part of you knows a case is built and not merely felt. You are the person who notices when someone is being squeezed, and you do not stay quiet about it. People learn that you can be approached, that you will hear the whole story and then say the true thing. The Moon keeps the cause personal, which is the gift and the rub. Your sense of justice rises and falls with your sympathies, and righteous anger is still anger; it can enjoy itself, and it can pick fights that belong to someone else. The reader in the old image is your corrective. Feeling tells you where to stand; study tells you how. When both are working, you become genuinely dangerous to bullies and genuinely safe for everyone else.

Peace, in the middle face of Libra, comes with a fence around it, and Saturn rules here. The tradition gives these degrees a strange double picture: two men in open fury, and a third man well dressed, seated calmly in a chair. The books say the face signifies indignation against evil, and also quietness, security, and a life furnished with plenty. Hold both halves, because you live both. Your idea of peace is not soft focus; it is a defended order. You want the household solvent, the promises kept, the standards enforced, and your anger, when it comes, has Saturn's temperature: cold, reasoned, and hard to talk down. People learn not to mistake your even voice for a flexible position. The risk is the pair of furious men. Judgment can become the pleasure here, a habit of sentencing what you were only asked to witness, and the comfortable chair can start to feel like something the world owes you. The tradition built its remedy into the pairing. Indignation belongs aimed at genuine wrong, and the quiet, well-provisioned life is the point of the defense, not a prize separate from it. The face keeps its promise when your firmness buys calm for more people than you, when the chair stays a chair and never quite becomes a bench.

The last face of Libra belongs to Jupiter, and the old books do not quite approve of it. Their picture shows a violent man with a bow, a naked man standing before him, and a third figure holding bread in one hand and a cup of wine in the other, and the meanings they list run to lust, song, sport, and gluttony. Read past the disapproval and you will recognize the territory: this is the part of the Scales where pleasure lives. Your appetite for the good things, company, music, food, flirtation, play, comes with a real talent for procuring them, for yourself and for a whole table. People have more fun when you are running the evening. You will want to sit with the naked man in the picture. Appetite this charming can consume. Someone else can end up exposed while you are entertained, and the line between conviviality and using people is one you cross more easily than you admit. The bread and wine are the tradition's own answer. What is held in both hands is meant to be given, and the face comes into its own when the pleasure you generate is one everyone present actually gets to share, including the person it was aimed at.

Mars is the ruler of the first face of Scorpio, and Mars is the sign's own master besides, so these degrees come at full strength. The old books picture them as a handsome woman being struck by two men, and their list of meanings runs in two directions at once: comeliness and beauty on one side, strife, treachery, deceit, and slander on the other. Put them together and you have the face's hard lesson: what is lovely and visible in you can attract blows. You may have learned this early. Something about your presence draws strong reactions, admiration and resentment arriving in the same package, and you have probably been punished for qualities you never flaunted. So you built the Scorpion's famous defenses. You test people before you show them much. You keep your real life out of view, and you can spot a false friend the way others spot a changed haircut. The defenses work, and that is the problem. A life organized around expecting betrayal starts inviting it, and striking first is still striking. The old picture holds a quieter fact: the woman in it has not withdrawn from view. Your courage is exactly that, staying visible, staying lovely, and letting discernment, rather than armor, decide who gets close.

The old image for Scorpio's middle face is an uncomfortable scene: a naked man and a naked woman, and a seated man watching two dogs bite each other in front of him. Its ruler is the Sun, and the books give the scene a hard reading: impudence, deceit, false dealing, mischief stirred up among people. Take it as the warning it is meant to be. What these degrees actually hand you is X-ray vision. Very little shocks you. You see what is underneath, the motive behind the courtesy, the quarrel under the agreement, and you can look at naked facts, your own included, without flinching. That is a genuine power, and like most powers in this sign it has a fork in it. There sits the fork, in the man who only watches. Watching conflict can become a taste. You can find yourself stirring the dogs, passing along the poisonous bit of news, keeping score of everyone's weaknesses for later. Or the same eyes can do the opposite: name the true thing in the room, refuse the false deal, and stay seated while everyone else is biting. The Sun's part in this face is honesty. Your sight is only as clean as what you use it for, and in the moment, you usually know which man you are being.

The last face of Scorpio is where desire proves stronger than the desirer. Venus, of all rulers, holds these degrees. The old picture has a man brought down to his knees with a woman raising a staff over him, and the books list drunkenness, lust, wrath, violence, and strife, which is their way of saying the same thing. You know something about it. Your wants do not arrive as preferences; they arrive as weather systems. Love, drink, anger, the need to merge or to win: any of them can pick you up and set you down somewhere you did not plan to be, and the morning after has its own education. The tradition is not sneering, though. Venus is still the ruler, and what kneels can also kneel willingly. The same capacity for total surrender, aimed at a person or a practice worthy of it, becomes devotion, the kind that transforms rather than degrades. The staff lands as consequence, and it teaches. You learn which of your hungers feed you and which eat you, mostly by being eaten a few times. What grows here, slowly, is someone who has been mastered by appetite and can therefore meet anyone's weakness without contempt, and whose yes, when it finally comes, means everything.
